claims.text: Equiatomic disordered FeCoNi has an FCC structure, high saturation magnetization, and low coercivity.
Introducing approximately 0.5 at.% interstitial nitrogen into FeCoNi can increase its coercivity.
Interstitial nitrogen causes local lattice distortion in FeCoNi.
Interstitial nitrogen increases the stacking-fault energy of the FCC FeCoNi matrix.
In equiatomic FCC CoCrNi, 0.5 at.% interstitial nitrogen increases stacking-fault energy.
In CoCrNi, 0.5 at.% nitrogen increases stacking-fault energy from about 22 to 42–44 mJ·m−2.
Higher stacking-fault energy reduces twin nucleation and increases the critical stress for deformation twinning.
Suppressing twinning through increased stacking-fault energy produces a more distorted FeCoNi lattice.
Nitrogen-induced lattice distortion creates stronger domain-wall pinning sites in FeCoNi.
Strong domain-wall pinning impedes domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal and thereby raises coercivity.
Nitrogen-doped FeCoNi will have higher coercivity than FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
Nitrogen-doped FeCoNi will retain high saturation magnetization.
FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt exhibit soft ferromagnetism with low coercivity.
Keeping the three metals equiatomic gives the alloy a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R.
Nitrogen content within its solubility limit can produce uniform interstitial occupation in an FCC FeCoNi lattice at room temperature.
Excessive nitrogen may produce unwanted phases or precipitates that compromise magnetic properties.
The coercivity response may depend on nitrogen concentration, processing conditions, and additional microstructural factors.

contradictions.description: The stated comparative outcome and baseline use FeCoNiPd/FeCoNiPt, whereas the experiment and falsification rule compare nitrogen-doped FeCoNi only with undoped ternary FeCoNi. Thus the proposed experiment does not directly test the principal claimed superiority over the prior derivatives.
